1.history: A small harbour town and the seat of the greatest house of Òrd na Cloiche, a low stone hall behind the harbour with the Stone's own mark cut plain over the door and nothing of the state's arms on it. In the twenty-first year the order rebuilt the house at its own cost and raised a low tower over its western gable, and hung in it a bell cast, the priests said, from coin given by every ship that had put in at the harbour and come home again. It is not a large bell, nor heard much past the town walls, but the town needed nothing heard past them: from that year the bell rang the hours, the market opened by it, and the harbour court and the fair court both sat by it, until within a year nobody in the town reckoned the time any other way.
1.known_for: the Stone's bell that rings the hours

255.history: A walled town of some size on the road east out of Cathair dhearg, its citadel old and its market square older. Oighrig nic Mhathain kept the weighing-scales of its market nine years and caught short weight better-paid men missed, until in the twenty-first year the council's eastern factor made her toll-mistress of the new fair at Muileann òg; she left her scales to a niece she had trained two summers. The carpenters of the town roofed the fair's court, a plain frame open on three sides, a fortnight before the first fair. In am Faoilleach of the twenty-second year the last stretch of the fair's road was metalled past the town, and the toll taken at its gate built a new wall along its southern side by an Lùnastal, which the townsfolk called the fair's wall and the carters called by their own name for the gate.
255.known_for: Oighrig's scales, and the fair's wall

18.history: A town of the east coast, past the last of the shires the Crown garrisoned closely, below which the Abhainn chaol meets the sea. The houses of the Seann Spioradan there had never had a hall of their own, only the hearth of whichever family kept the year's rite. In the twenty-second year forty households raised a common hall in a single season, working the stone by day, and roofed it before the first frost; it holds no image or carving, only two hearths. At its first naming forty heads of houses spoke the names of their dead, one old woman of the town reciting nine generations before her son finished the tenth, and the chronicler Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill rode east to watch. From the next year the hall sent the Library a copy of its naming every year, a little longer each time. In the sixty-eighth and sixty-ninth years the herring did not come to the grounds off the river mouth, and the town's boats went north.

119.history: A town far up the eastern coast, past even Seann Dunn, which had none of the five lighthouses the humans left the kingdom to keep. It had a mole built in the humans' time for a fleet larger than the one that used it. After two boats were lost on the harbour rocks in a winter fog, its council voted in the twenty-third year to burn a light on the end of the mole with coal bought out of the town's own purse. It asked the Lighthouse Board to take the light on, and the Board wrote back that its charter named five lights and no more, and that the town's light, being no charge on the Crown, might continue as it was; the chronicler entered the refusal in four lines. The light burned on the town's coal. When the coal line shut in the thirty-fourth year the town lived on its stored coal.

22.history: A town of the south where the droves from Muileann fhionn came down to market and where the fair-wardens grazed the fair's horses on rising ground outside the walls. In the twenty-third year the wardens called an old custom of arms the Còmhrag, the melee, and fought it on that field, drawing men from every vein-town within two days' walk; Calum Ruadh of Muileann chrom won it, took a year's wages and the right to bear arms, and four inn-keepers who had built new houses for the crowd kept his table free. Two men died in the first and six in the thirty-sixth year, and the wardens refused the custodians' petition to end it within the hour; the circus pitched on the trampled ground a week after the six burials. The coal line reached the town the same season and its quays spread half a mile past the old gate. Ealasaid nic Coinnich of Àth ghlas won it in the forty-fifth year and did not fight again; edged iron was banned from the ring in the fifty-fourth. By the fifty-seventh year its coal quays stood half idle and the wardens raised the gate-price.

24.history: A fishing town of the north-central coast. In the twenty-fourth year it gave over its whole spring to a dock long enough to take three grain-ships abreast, for the Hawk country had begun to send its barley and oats down by water rather than by cart. The Hawk houses blessed the dock and asked a tithe of its dues; the shire's factor haggled them down to a twentieth and paid it, and has paid it every quarter since, so that the clerks of the town call the due simply the Hawk's and few of them can say why a fishing town owes a grain due to a bird that flies inland. Northern boats that landed fish at the new dock paid the same twentieth out of the Moot's harbour purse, which Mary Coyle raised in the Moot the first night she stood up to speak.
24.known_for: the grain dock and the Hawk's twentieth

110.history: The Seann Bhral of the southern coast, not the older town of the name in the west, which is a different town and always has been. In the twenty-fourth year it passed Ros dhomhain in the weight of fish landed and became the greatest fishing port of the kingdom; its curing-sheds, which had been four, became eleven and ran the whole length of the harbour, so that a stranger walking it after dark could follow the smell of the smoke from end to end. Fish from it went up to the capital through Ceann mhin's covered market. In the sixty-first and sixty-second years the three great pumps of the Sloc Mòr came to it by rail from above Achadh dhomhain to drain its new dry dock.
110.known_for: the curing-sheds, and the Sloc Mòr's pumps

29.history: A town of the capital shore. In the twenty-seventh year its glass-houses, which had lately begun blowing small flasks, found a trade no one had planned for them: the women of the town filled the flasks with waters they distilled themselves from bog-myrtle and meadowsweet and heather honey and sold them by the dozen, and within a few years scent was sold in every market town. A cloth trader out of the town, putting in at Cuan shean, offered Harry Marlow a northern passage in the fourteenth year, which Harry refused. Two of its masons drove and cemented the iron reef post at Tobar dhearg for Ciorstaidh nic Artair in the fifty-fifth year, working only the hour either side of the ebb. The glass-houses still stand, and the scent trade still runs from them.

371.history: A town on the Abhainn ìseal in the north-central country, a river port of storehouses. In the twenty-ninth year fire took its warehouse quarter, three storehouses and a dozen dwellings above them, and burned two days before the town beat it back street by street with buckets and wet sacking and a chain of hands to the river; no one died. The town's Hawk house, which had never taken in households outside those sworn to it, sheltered every family the fire put out of a roof, sworn or not, through the spring cold. The council bought the town a bell from the founders' yard at Cathair dhearg to stand where the old warehouse bell burned, and rang it once on the quay before it was hung; by the town's own telling it is heard further up and down the river than any bell in the kingdom.
371.known_for: the fire and the loudest bell

324.history: A harbour town of the south-west on the road between Cathair dhomhain and Seann Bhral, where Eilidh nic Leòid's circuit passed. A grave-list from the town was among the first papers the chronicler copied fair, and a wedding there went into the chronicle beside Brìghde's death. In the thirtieth year it built its own harbour, the first raised anywhere in the kingdom since the Severance without a coin of the Crown's in it, the house of the Stone lending against the town's dues and the masons building the mole to the Stone's measure; the house took its first quarter's dues off the quay before the last course was dry. A fishing boat of the town struck the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg in the fifty-fourth year, and the keeper Artair mac Mhurchaidh drowned bringing in her crew; the town's fishing families paid half the reef bell that followed.
324.known_for: the harbour built on the Stone's loan

492.history: A salt town on the tidal flats of the east coast below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, worked by Dia-thìreach ford-keepers, its boats crewed as often by Tuathaich hands as not. Its flats were dug for salt-pans in the thirty-second year and it was soon supplying salt up the coast. In an Gearran of the forty-fourth year flagless ships came in under cloud and burned its three salt-sheds; the patrol came two days late, and the households judged the captain's honest report an accounting that answered every question but the one that mattered. The sheds were raised again within the year, the Crown paying a third. An old salt-carrier on its quay gave Murchadh mac Coinnich the coast's names for the raiders' hulls, An Ròn Dubh and An Fhaoileag, which the royal chronicle took from the keeper's own log. Mòrag nic Coinnich was made the Library's deputy on the road home from it.
492.known_for: the salt-sheds burned, and the raiders named

297.history: A town of the southern plain. In the thirty-third year the Crown's grain-store here was finished, two winters building and one summer roofing, a hall of dressed stone long enough that a loaded cart could turn inside it, great enough to feed the south a season, filled from the south's own harvests. It opened its doors first in a poor season that same year, and in the forty-third it fed the dry country about Achadh shean, its grain reaching the sidings there by the coal line on the morning of the first rain. In the sixty-third year the harvest came in so thick that the maor wrote to Muileann chaol of granaries built for a lean year wanting a second storey, and Tormod Pinn struck through his own note of a hungry year to come.

304.history: A town an easy day's ride from Caol mhòr, seat of a northern shire. Its maor's chest was the one the northern shires filled for the first chronicle circuit in the nineteenth year, and Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill found in it the maor's returns and nothing more, not a line in a Tuathaich hand, and wrote the fact down without a further word. Eachann mac Rath practised physic here twenty years under his guild's charter. In the thirty-fourth year he took Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch, two women of the fishing country, to learn by watching him set bones and mix poultices through a fever season; a factor's wife let slip at a fair stall that his new girls handled a lancet as steady as he did, and the guild struck him from its rolls. He kept his surgery open all the same.

25.history: A town of the Hawk country in Siorrachd Cnoc bheag, whose altar Raonaid nic Iain's mother's mother kept before her. In an Cèitean of the thirty-fifth year the Hawk houses met in its hall and named Raonaid custodian of their own by standing up house by house, and Murchadh Ruadh gave her a white feather kept three generations in his house. The letter from Seann Skell refusing to own her was read once in the hall and put away, not burned. Here she wrote the Hawk's spoken order into a farm account-book, read it aloud once at the full moon of an t-Samhain, and locked it in the iron box that had held the altar's lamp-oil, wearing the key on a cord under her shawl. The shire's new seal of a white hawk was brought to it in the thirty-sixth year.

63.history: A harbour of the west coast where Walter Hale clerked the humans' harbour office twenty years before the crossing closed. In the first year the council shut the humans' chapel here for good and carted its bell north, and households were walked north out of the town under guard; the bell hung at last in Cnoc ghorm's tower. Agnes Pike copied herring and salt tallies in its harbour agent's office for a dozen years. Its harbour would not give Mary Coyle's eleven boats its quay in the twenty-fifth year and sent them to a mooring buoy off the point. In the thirty-sixth year a coal-ship yard was opened here, and the eldest masters of Ros dhomhain lost their protest against it before the guild court.
63.known_for: Walter Hale's harbour, and the chapel bell

8.history: The Dùn thais of the west coast, within a morning's ride of Ros bheag; there are two towns of the name, and the record keeps them apart as west and east. Its fishermen settled salvage among themselves by custom until a wrecked raider's hulk driven ashore proved too rich a prize for custom to divide, and in the thirty-seventh year the town was granted a court of the sea of its own to judge salvage and wreck along its shore. At its first sitting, held on the strand, the court awarded the hulk whole to the crews who drove it aground. For ten years the royal record confused its court with the eastern town's market, until Tormod Pinn marked the two west and east in the forty-eighth year.

77.history: The Dùn thais of the east, seat of its own shire and its own dues; the other town of the name lies on the west coast. In the thirty-eighth year it raised at the shire's own charge a long timbered covered market for the hill farms that had traded in its square uncovered since the town was walled, and its first trading was held under a roof that smelled more of new-cut wood than of the grain it sheltered. A clerk at Cathair dhearg filed its petition and the western town's against the one name, and the royal record confused the two for ten years until Tormod Pinn ruled a line through the record marking them west and east.

346.history: A gathering of pits and shanties in the western hills where Tuathaich hewers had worked the coal since before the kingdom drew a road to them. In the thirteenth year the Rail Board built a spur of thirteen miles to it off the western branch, because the coal was cheap to lift and the carters' road worse each winter. After the fall at Muileann dhearg the Board's new timbering rule was posted on its pit-head door and the timber ordered from Ceann mhòr, and the timber never came; the hewers went on under the old props, and Mary Coyle named the town in her letter to the Board. In the sixty-eighth year the Board withdrew its overseers and the branch together, and the pits passed to the hewers, who chose captains, weighed every cart and set by the Crown's fifth under the Leòid ruling; the Board entered the payments as arrears. The Board's factors at its railhead, the nearest to the north, refused the Doire ghlas mill's cloth in the fifty-ninth year and weighed its first bale onto the line in the sixtieth. From the sixty-ninth year its coal went to Seann Bhral by cart.
